fraught

/FRAWT/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Fraught means filled or loaded with something difficult, tense, or dangerous — almost always in the pattern 'fraught with ___'

Fraught means filled or loaded with something difficult, tense, or dangerous — it almost always appears in the pattern 'fraught with.' The peace negotiations were fraught with mistrust, and both delegations nearly walked out twice.

Example

The family reunion was fraught with old grudges, and every toast seemed one wrong word away from an argument.

Fraught with tells you the gathering was loaded with tension — the old grudges filled the event the way cargo fills a ship, and the word warns you the load is a troublesome one.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

laden: Laden means weighed down with a heavy load, and the load can be anything — a ship laden with cargo, a table laden with food, a voice laden with meaning. Fraught takes only one kind of cargo: trouble. A fraught situation is loaded with tension, risk, or danger, never with anything welcome.

charged: Charged describes an atmosphere crackling with suppressed emotion, like static before a storm — a charged silence, a charged glance. Fraught is broader about the trouble it carries: a situation can be fraught with risk, delays, or danger with no emotion in the room at all. Charged means feeling; fraught means trouble of any kind.

riddled: Riddled means shot through with flaws that are already there — a report riddled with errors, a wall riddled with holes. Fraught looks forward as much as inward: a fraught crossing is loaded with what could go wrong. Riddled counts the defects present; fraught measures the trouble hanging over the whole undertaking.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

tranquil: calm and peaceful

carefree: free of worry or trouble

Where it sits · how serious the trouble gets

tricky → fraught → perilous

tricky vs. fraught: A tricky situation has a few snags to work around; a fraught one is loaded with tension at every turn.

perilous vs. fraught: A fraught crossing is loaded with risk; a perilous one puts lives in immediate danger.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — fraught: from Middle Dutch vracht, 'cargo, freight' — literally 'loaded'

Put it together: Fraught began as the Middle Dutch word vracht, 'cargo': a ship fraught with goods was fully loaded. English kept the loading idea but changed the cargo to trouble — a situation fraught with danger is loaded with it.

Use the root in a new word: freight: The freight cars were loaded with grain — freight and fraught both grew from the same old word for a ship's cargo.

Root Check

Word Choice

Formal / literary

Fraught nearly always travels with 'with' — fraught with danger, fraught with tension, fraught with risk. Modern English also allows a bare use ('a fraught relationship'), where it simply means tense. Either way, the load is always trouble: fraught never describes happy abundance.
